newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protestors defy warning on Belgrade marches.
newsitem.headline: Protestors defy warning on Belgrade marches.

text.p: Opponents of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic defied a police warning and marched against the government in Belgrade on Thursday, daring authorities to crack down on nearly six weeks of street protests.

About 5,000 students assembled in the city centre at midday for what has become a ritual daily procession through Belgrade to the sound of beating drums, blaring trumpets, shrill whistles and anti-Milosevic chants.
Icy, snow-packed streets and sub-freezing temperatures reduced the size of the student protest but did little to diminish its carnival-like atmosphere.
A larger daily march organized by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition was scheduled for mid afternoon in the capital.
The Ministry of Interior issued an ambiguously worded statement on Wednesday which seemed to say that any protest which obstructed traffic would be banned.
The students shifted the start of their march to a pedestrian street, maintaining a non-confrontational approach towards the police.

Police on the scene warned that any attempt by the students to move through the city would produce a response. After some deliberation student leaders announced they would proceed with the march after a series of speeches concluded.
There was no immediate sign of the riot police who intervened on Tuesday to separate clashing crowds of pro- and anti- Milosevic forces who fought running skirmishes in the streets.
At least 58 people were injured in Tuesday's melee, including one man who was shot and critically wounded by a Milosevic supporter.
The anti-government protests began after Milosevic and his ruling SPS party refused to accept a stunning series of opposition victories in local elections on November 17.

The opposition seemed confident on Thursday that broad support among ordinary citizens would prevent police from enforcing a ban on marches in Belgrade, where tens of thousands of people have been demonstrating daily.
"Some time ago the police issued a similar statement but did nothing to act upon it we expect the same thing to happen this time," student spokesperson Mira Milosevic told Reuters.
Vuk Draskovic, leader of the opposition Serbian Renewal Movement, said any violence would be Milosevic's fault.

"This responsibility will be Milosevic's because if the police and Milosevic's drunken and armed people were not on the streets there would not be any problems at all," Draskovic said in a radio interview.

Opposition protests had gone ahead without violence for weeks until Milosevic and the SPS transported supporters from outside Belgrade into the city on Tuesday for a rally at the same time and place as the daily opposition march.
Europe and the United States have warned Milosevic that further violence against the protestors could thwart Belgrade's ambitions to reintegrate Serbia and Yugoslavia with Europe.
Russia, traditionally more sympathetic to Serbia than the west, has warned against outside any interference in Belgrade's current political turmoil.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe is expected to deliver its opinion on the outcome of Serbia's November 17 local elections within the next few days.
